source: Ramanujan, Sabharwal, Selman (2010) On Adversarial Search Spaces and Sampling-Based Planning (ICAPS)
finding: Shallow search traps (a short forced loss for the player to move) are common in chess but rare in Go. UCT does not separate a trap move from the best move, while minimax does.
numbers: In 200 semi-random chess games about 7-10% of games at 15 to 31 plies had a trap at levels 1-7, up to 15% at 47 plies. In 200 grandmaster games about 12% at 47 plies. Traps exist at depths as low as 3 to 7. For level-5 and level-7 traps the UCT value of the trap move stays very close to the best move over the first 100,000 iterations; only the level-3 trap was identified.
quote: UCT, unlike minimax search, is unable to identify such traps in Chess
limits: Chess-specific. UCT bias 0.4, plain playouts. Later work (AlphaZero) shows a learned evaluator can avoid many traps.
agent_relevance: A search that averages samples can rate a fatal branch almost as good as the best branch. Our agent should not trust averaged sample agreement where one wrong step is fatal; it needs an exact check on the short forced line.

source: Ramanujan, Sabharwal, Selman (2010) Understanding Sampling Style Adversarial Search Methods (UAI)
finding: On synthetic game trees UCT's success depends on tree structure. Success in Go did not transfer to chess. Informed playouts between weak minimax players gave mixed gains.
numbers: No single headline number was extracted from the text read (synthetic trees plus chess with heuristic values).
limits: Search-space structure explains much of the gap, not the algorithm alone.
agent_relevance: Before using tree search, ask whether the task has early losses (trap-like) or only late ones. Tasks with early irreversible errors are the bad case for sampling search.

source: Ramanujan, Selman (2011) Trade-Offs in Sampling-Based Adversarial Planning (ICAPS)
finding: In Mancala UCT is compared part by part with minimax. The paper says attempts to repeat UCT's Go success in other games were largely unsuccessful and studies what each UCT part contributes.
numbers: Game: Mancala. Win-rate tables were not extracted in this session.
limits: Single game; numbers not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Component ablation (selection rule, playout, backup) is the right way to test any search piece we add.

source: Coquelin, Munos (2007) Bandit Algorithms for Tree Search
finding: UCT can be over-optimistic. Its worst-case regret can be very poor, with a dependence on depth D that is a tower of exponentials.
numbers: Paper states a double-exponential dependence on depth in the worst case and proposes alternative bandit algorithms (BAST, flat UCB) with better worst cases when tree smoothness is known.
quote: UCT is over-optimistic in some sense, leading to a worst-case regret that may be very poor
limits: Worst-case theory. Average behaviour in Go was good in practice.
agent_relevance: Deep narrow reasoning chains with a rare right path are the worst case for UCT-style exploration. Prefer wide shallow sampling with exact checks.

source: Baier, Winands (2018) MCTS-Minimax Hybrids with State Evaluations (JAIR 62, 193-231)
finding: MCTS with selective sampling and averaged backups easily misses or underestimates an important move in tactical games with many terminal states and shallow traps. Embedding shallow minimax searches into MCTS repairs this.
numbers: Abstract says MCTS is susceptible to traps because of selective sampling and averaging value backups. Text adds that MCTS is still more susceptible to traps than alpha-beta whatever the evaluator.
quote: MCTS is still more susceptible to traps than alpha-beta
limits: Game domains; hybrids add cost per node.
agent_relevance: Mix cheap exact lookahead (a code check) inside sampled search at the points where one error is fatal.

source: Silver et al. (2017) Mastering Chess and Shogi by Self-Play with a General RL Algorithm (AlphaZero)
finding: MCTS with a learned policy and value net beat Stockfish in chess, so the trap weakness can be largely offset by a strong learned evaluator.
numbers: Paper reports AlphaZero outperformed Stockfish after training (exact game counts not copied here).
limits: Needs a value net trained by self-play, which a no-training scaffold lacks.
agent_relevance: The trap problem is eased by a good value function. We have none, so an LLM-judged value is the weak point (see later lines).

source: Wang, Gleave et al. (2023) Adversarial Policies Beat Superhuman Go AIs (ICML)
finding: An adversary that does not play Go well beats superhuman KataGo by tricking its evaluation (cyclic groups it thinks are safe). Search reduces but does not remove the exploit.
numbers: Pass-adversary: 99.9% win at 600 adversary visits vs Latest with no search. Cyclic-adversary: 95.7% (1052 games) vs defended Latest at 4096 visits; 97.3% (1000 games) vs undefended at 4096 visits; 72% vs Latest at 10^7 visits. Human experts can copy the attack.
quote: the core vulnerability uncovered by our attack persists even in KataGo agents adversarially trained
limits: Go-specific. The blind spot is the value net, not search depth.
agent_relevance: Search cannot fix a bad evaluator: more visits did not close the blind spot. For us, more samples from the same model do not fix a correlated blind spot.

source: Tseng, McLean, Pelrine, Wang, Gleave (2024) Can Go AIs be adversarially robust?
finding: Adversarial training, a vision-transformer network and other defenses did not fully patch KataGo; new adversaries beat each defended version cheaply.
numbers: Adversary win rate against the adversarially trained dec23-victim fell to 0% then a fine-tuned adversary got 91% (512 visits) with 6% of the victim's training compute and 65% at 4096 visits. Atari variant wins 81% at 512 visits with under 5% of compute. a9 wins 42% vs v9 even at 65,536 visits. ViT-victim lost 78% to a fine-tuned cyclic attack.
limits: Go; the claim is that robustness is hard to get by training alone.
agent_relevance: A patched system can keep the same weakness. Re-test fixes with a fresh attacker, not the cases used to patch.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with LLMs
finding: Search over thoughts with LLM self-evaluation lifts Game of 24 far above chain of thought; breadth helps.
numbers: Game of 24 with GPT-4: IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC 9.0%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%.
quote: while GPT-4 with chain-of-thought prompting only solved 4% of tasks, our method achieved a success rate of 74%
limits: Short tasks (3 steps in Game of 24). Costs many more calls. Later work shows self-evaluation is unreliable on deeper tasks.
agent_relevance: Shallow breadth search with a model-judged value works on short problems with clear pruning. This is the safe regime for our scaffold.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: MCTS with the LLM as world model and reward lifts Blocksworld planning; 64% average success while chain of thought nearly fails; 33% relative gain over CoT with GPT-4.
numbers: RAP also beats CoT+SC on a math word task (94.2 vs 89.8 in a table read). More rollouts help (RAP(20) above RAP(10) in the Blocksworld table).
limits: Blocksworld has a clean state and action model. Depth is capped near 7, as noted by Feng et al.
agent_relevance: MCTS helps when state transitions can be simulated reliably. Use it only when transitions are checkable by code.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning (LATS)
finding: MCTS over ReAct-style actions with LM value and reflection gives top results on HumanEval. The paper states two limits: higher compute cost, and the need to revert to earlier states.
numbers: HumanEval Pass@1 92.7% with GPT-4; WebShop average score +22.1 with GPT-3.5.
quote: LATS assumes the ability to revert to earlier states in decision-making environments
limits: Assumes the environment can be reset to a previous state, which fails for irreversible actions.
agent_relevance: Direct trap-state warning: tree search with backtracking is unsafe where actions cannot be undone. Add a rule never to search by acting in irreversible environments.

source: Feng et al. (2023) AlphaZero-Like Tree-Search can Guide LLM Decoding and Training (TS-LLM)
finding: Prompt-based self-evaluation value functions are not always reliable; a learned value net from a 7B model can beat GPT-3.5 prompting as a value. ToT and RAP are capped at depth 10 or 7. TS-LLM handles depth 64.
numbers: Among BFS, DFS and MCTS with an outcome reward model, MCTS is almost the best on performance and compute, so value backpropagation matters. Simple CoT-SC is competitive when the search space is small.
limits: Learned value needs training data. Tasks: Game24, GSM8K, PrOntoQA, RLHF alignment.
agent_relevance: Judging nodes by prompting the same LLM is the soft spot. Prefer code checks as the value signal.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1, appendix: unsuccessful attempts with MCTS
finding: MCTS for training failed to scale. Token generation has an exponentially larger search space than chess; capping node expansion traps the model in local optima; a fine-grained value model is very hard to train.
numbers: Authors conclude MCTS with a pre-trained value model can improve inference, but iteratively improving the model by self-search is a significant challenge. Another appendix note says majority voting lifts R1 from 79.8% to 86.7% (AIME 2024) and that MCTS can complement long reasoning.
quote: iteratively boosting model performance through self-search remains a significant challenge
limits: Negative result reported without numbers for the MCTS runs.
agent_relevance: A frontier lab dropped MCTS for long reasoning. Use the simplest scaffold that gives checkable signals.

source: Wu, Sun, Li, Welleck, Yang (2025) Inference Scaling Laws (ICLR)
finding: MCTS is costly and pairs badly with weighted voting because it yields many unfinished solutions. A cheaper tree search (REBASE) wins.
numbers: MCTS often needs dozens of times more generated tokens than best-of-n or majority voting. REBASE beat sampling and MCTS in all settings; Llemma-7B with REBASE matched Llemma-34B with 2x less FLOPs on MATH500 and beat Llemma-34B with majority voting at all budgets.
quote: MCTS consumes substantially more resources, often requiring dozens of times more generated tokens
limits: Math, reward-model guided. REBASE is the authors' own method.
agent_relevance: At equal tokens, sampling plus voting often beats MCTS. Spend tokens on diverse samples with checks, not on rollouts that never become answers.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally
finding: Reward-model-guided search helps on hard problems and hurts on easy ones. Beam search beats best-of-N at small budgets but gains fade; lookahead search underperforms most because search exploits reward-model errors.
numbers: Compute-optimal adaptive strategy beats best-of-N using about 4x less test-time compute. On MATH levels 1-2 beam search degrades as budget rises; on levels 3-4 it beats best-of-N; on level 5 no method makes meaningful progress. Over-optimized search gives repetitive or 1-2 step answers.
limits: PaLM 2 with a PRM on MATH.
agent_relevance: Stronger optimisation against a learned judge gives worse answers (Goodhart). Match search strength to difficulty and cap it.

source: Qin, Alvarez-Melis, Jelassi, Malach (2025) To Backtrack or Not to Backtrack (COLM)
finding: At a fixed token budget, sequential search with backtracking in the chain of thought loses to parallel sampling on CountDown but wins on Sudoku.
numbers: CountDown: 1,152 search paths per game, DFS solver gets 57% of 500k questions. Sudoku: DFS gets 97% of boards. After GRPO the backtracking model reaches nearly 70% at 4096 tokens (above the 57% teacher); the direct model after GRPO gets 42.5% pass@1 (82 of 200).
limits: Small models trained from scratch on synthetic tasks; result depends on task structure.
agent_relevance: Backtracking is not universally better; training on fixed search traces locks in poor strategies. Prefer parallel diverse attempts when many routes lead in.

source: Inoue et al. (2025) Wider or Deeper? Adaptive Branching Tree Search (AB-MCTS, NeurIPS spotlight)
finding: Fixed-width standard MCTS is often no better than repeated sampling for code and ARC-AGI. Letting each node go wider or deeper adaptively beats both.
numbers: ARC-AGI: repeated sampling is a strong baseline. MLE-Bench average rank: AB-MCTS-M 1.3, sequential refinement 2.3, repeated sampling 3.0, standard MCTS 3.3 (last of four).
limits: GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3; small budgets; authors' own method.
agent_relevance: Plain MCTS ranked last of four. Sample wide first and deepen only on a signal (fits G1).

source: Zhang, Wei, Jiang, Pan, Shu, Liu (2026) Cost-Awareness in Tree-Search LLM Planning
finding: On budgeted planning, ToT-BFS, DFS, MCTS and bidirectional search: more search compute does not reliably give optimal plans. MCTS is best on short horizons, bidirectional search best overall.
numbers: Failure modes under tight budgets: ToT-BFS 98% search exhaustion, DFS 92% exhaustion, MCTS 52% exhaustion and 48% budget violation, bidirectional search 92% budget violation.
limits: Blocksworld-style planning with action costs; LLM scorers.
agent_relevance: Search finds a valid plan and still breaks the cost limit because the LLM value is blind to cost. Make costs explicit in code.

source: Koh, McAleer, Fried, Salakhutdinov (2025) Tree Search for Language Model Agents (TMLR)
finding: Best-first search in a live web environment helps agents and scales with compute, but is slow and needs resettable states.
numbers: VisualWebArena: +39.7% relative with GPT-4o, to 26.4% success. WebArena: +28.0% relative, to 19.2%. A search budget c=20 can use up to 20x more LM calls.
limits: Destructive actions are blocked by design; real sites cannot always be reset.
agent_relevance: Gains of 28-40% relative are real but cost up to 20x calls. Use search only at chosen decision points.

source: Stroebl, Kapoor, Narayanan (2026 version) The Limits of Inference Scaling Through Resampling
finding: Resampling against an imperfect verifier cannot beat the verifier's false-positive rate, whatever the compute.
numbers: On HumanEval and MBPP single-sample accuracy correlates with false-positive rate; the best number of samples is often under 10, after which curves bend downward.
limits: Code with weak unit tests.
agent_relevance: A check we trust must be strong. This is guardrail G3: a pass must be on held-out tests.

source: Rethinking Inference-Time Scaling: Efficiency Limits and Linguistic Signals (arXiv 2504.14047 v2)
finding: Non-reasoning models hit a reasoning floor that more inference compute cannot cross. Among reasoning models, simple majority voting beats sequential revision and mixture-of-agents.
numbers: Correct responses are shorter with fewer hedging markers; the paper uses these as zero-compute quality proxies. Other numbers not extracted.
limits: Abstract and intro read.
agent_relevance: Voting beats elaborate search-like scaffolds for strong models; keep the loop simple.

source: Qwen Team (2025) The Lessons of Developing Process Reward Models in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: Monte Carlo rollout estimates of step correctness give worse PRMs than LLM-as-judge or human labels, because rollouts can reach right answers from wrong steps. Best-of-N evaluation of PRMs is biased.
numbers: Qualitative: many PRM minimum scores sit on the final answer step.
limits: Math PRMs.
agent_relevance: The MCTS value (rollout success) is a noisy estimate of step quality; do not use rollouts to certify steps.

source: Setlur et al. (2025) Scaling Test-Time Compute Without Verification or RL is Suboptimal
finding: Distilling search traces (verifier-free) scales worse than verifier-based RL or search at the same budget.
numbers: Proven gap grows with compute when the base model's correct traces are heterogeneous; checked with S1 distillation vs best-of-N.
limits: Theory plus small experiments.
agent_relevance: Verification is what makes search worth its cost.

source: PRM generalization from math to code in test-time scaling (arXiv 2506.00027)
finding: Process reward models trained on math carry over to code only in part; PRM-guided test-time scaling depends on the task.
numbers: Numbers not extracted in this session (abstract and intro only).
limits: Shallow read.
agent_relevance: Learned step judges do not transfer freely.

source: Qian et al. (2026) PAC-CF: Calibrating Irreversible Frontier Pruning in LLM-Guided Search
finding: Pruning low-scored branches in LLM-guided search turns biased scorer errors into irreversible losses; a calibrated gap threshold keeps a valid branch.
numbers: Three domains, five controllers, budgets B100 to B500; pruning-aware ToolTree gains +4.38 utility points at each tested budget; the macro-average CI excludes zero only at B100 and B200.
limits: Utility point estimates; CI excludes zero at two budgets only.
agent_relevance: Direct trap-state fix for LLM trees: never hard-prune on the model's score alone; calibrate the cutoff on held-out tasks.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks
finding: LLMs alone are poor planners and self-critics; pair them with external verifiers that critique candidate plans.
numbers: Position paper; no new benchmark numbers recorded here.
limits: Position paper.
agent_relevance: Supports code-checked transitions: the model proposes, the program verifies.

source: Orseau, Lelis (2018) Single-Agent Policy Tree Search With Guarantees
finding: Policy-guided tree search (LevinTS, LubyTS) gives bounds on search steps that PUCT-style search lacks.
numbers: Gives expansion bounds tied to node depth and inverse policy probability (theory).
limits: Single-agent deterministic puzzles.
agent_relevance: Bounded-cost search is a design target for our loop.

source: Kaufmann, Koolen (2017) Monte-Carlo Tree Search by Best Arm Identification
finding: UCT-style selection is not built for finding the best arm; best-arm-identification gives provable sample complexity.
numbers: Theory results only.
limits: Zero-sum game trees.
agent_relevance: Choosing where to spend samples is a bandit problem with better rules than UCB.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) ReST-MCTS*: LLM Self-Training via Process Reward Guided Tree Search
finding: Tree search with process reward self-trains the policy and beats PRM + best-of-N at matched budget by the authors' account.
numbers: Figure shows ReST-MCTS* above PRM+Best-of-N at matched budget; text says MCTS needs fewer tokens than SC and ORM+BoN at equal accuracy.
limits: Author claim; conflicts with the Wu et al. cost finding. Depends on how tokens are counted.
agent_relevance: Contested: MCTS token efficiency depends on who counts tokens.

source: Xie et al. (2024) Monte Carlo Tree Search Boosts Reasoning via Iterative Preference Learning
finding: MCTS-derived step values used to build preference pairs for training improve reasoning.
numbers: Numbers not extracted in this session.
limits: Training-time use, not an inference scaffold.
agent_relevance: MCTS is more useful for making training data than as a runtime loop.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Mutual Reasoning Makes Smaller LLMs Stronger Problem-Solvers (rStar)
finding: MCTS with a second small model as discriminator (mutual consistency) lifts small models; self-reward alone is unreliable.
numbers: GSM8K: LLaMA2-7B 12.51% to 63.91%; Mistral-7B 36.46% to 81.88%; LLaMA3-8B-Instruct 74.53% to 91.13%; 32 rollouts. Only 24% of RAP trajectories from LLaMA2-7B on GSM8K were judged correct.
limits: Gains measured over weak baselines; authors' own method.
agent_relevance: Agreement between two models gives a pruning signal, but G4 warns that samples from one model are not independent.
